Rethinking the Comparison Unit in Sequence-Level Reinforcement Learning: An Equal-Length Paired Training Framework from Loss Correction to Sample Construction

Fei Ding Affiliation: Alibaba Group    Yongkang Zhang Affiliation: Alibaba Group    Runhao Liu Affiliation: Alibaba Group    Yuhao Liao Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Zijian Zeng Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Huiming Yang Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Sibo Wang Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Linglin Liao Affiliation: Tsinghua University
Abstract

This paper investigates the length problem in sequence-level relative reinforcement learning. We observe that, although existing methods partially alleviate length-related phenomena, a more fundamental issue remains insufficiently characterized: the comparison units used during training lack inherent comparability. Building on this observation, we propose a new perspective: the length problem should not be viewed merely as a loss-scaling or normalization bias, but rather as a comparison unit construction problem. We further establish a sample-construction-based training framework that, instead of applying post-hoc corrections to unequal-length responses, proactively constructs equal-length, alignable, and comparable training segments during generation. Within this framework, we propose EqLen, a concrete method applicable to group-relative comparison algorithms such as GRPO, GSPO, and RLOO. Through dual-track synchronous generation, prefix inheritance, and segment masking, EqLen efficiently collects effective equal-length training segments and enables stable optimization.

1 Introduction

Sequence-level relative reinforcement learning has become a key technique for enhancing the complex reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Among these methods, group-relative comparison-based optimization approaches have attracted widespread attention due to their training stability, implementation simplicity, and reduced dependence on reward models. These methods typically assume that multiple candidate responses generated for the same question can be directly compared and jointly optimized based on their relative quality. However, a critical issue remains insufficiently characterized: whether these candidate responses inherently constitute directly comparable training units. In language model generation, different responses often exhibit substantial variation in length, termination position, and reasoning depth. Consequently, the optimization process compares not only answer quality but also conflates structural misalignment and scaling distortion introduced by length differences. In other words, the root cause of existing length problems may lie not only in how the objective function is corrected, but in whether the training comparison units themselves are comparable.

Building on this observation, we propose a new perspective: the length problem in sequence-level relative reinforcement learning should fundamentally be understood as a comparison unit construction problem, rather than merely a loss function correction problem. Existing work primarily mitigates length-related effects from the loss function side through reweighting, normalization, or length-scaling corrections. While these methods have achieved empirical progress, they still operate on direct comparisons of naturally unequal-length responses and therefore do not change the fact that comparison units are structurally misaligned. We argue that, rather than applying post-hoc compensation on incomparable samples, it is more effective to proactively construct more alignable and comparable training segments during generation. The length problem is thus reformulated as: how to design a training mechanism such that optimization is genuinely built upon structurally fair comparison units.

Based on this perspective, we further establish a sample-construction-based training framework whose core idea is: instead of directly comparing naturally unequal-length complete responses, we proactively construct equal-length, alignable, and comparable training segments during the generation process. This framework shifts the treatment of the length problem from passive correction on the loss side to active construction on the sample side, thereby making the definition of training signals clearer and the comparison relationships more consistent. Within this framework, we propose the concrete method EqLen. This method collects candidate trajectories through a dual-track synchronous generation mechanism. When one trajectory terminates early, the effective prefix of the other trajectory is used to continue constructing new comparison branches, and multiple effective equal-length training segments are collected at length-aligned positions. Furthermore, we introduce a segment masking mechanism that excludes inherited prefixes and invalid suffixes after pair expiration from gradient updates, so that policy optimization acts only on newly generated suffixes that genuinely participate in comparison. Through this approach, EqLen translates the new perspective of “comparison unit comparability” into an executable training mechanism, significantly improving training signal utilization efficiency while mitigating length-induced optimization distortion.

We propose a fundamentally different approach: rather than patching the loss function on unequal-length trajectories, we generate equal-length trajectories from the source. Our equal-length trajectory generation method (EqLen) modifies the inference framework itself: (1) Synchronous dual-track generation: groups are split into subgroups of size 2, with two trajectories decoded synchronously; (2) Prefix inheritance: when one trajectory terminates, the existing tokens of the other serve as a prefix to initialize a new trajectory for continued generation, and this process repeats; (3) Equal-length pairing: each “convergence point” naturally produces an equal-length trajectory pair that is directly used for training.

Figure 1 provides an intuitive comparison between EqLen and standard GRPO.

Our contributions are as follows:
  • •

    We identify a critical yet insufficiently characterized problem: the length phenomena in existing sequence-level relative reinforcement learning originate not merely from loss scaling or normalization bias, but from the fundamental lack of comparability of the training comparison units themselves.

  • •

    We reveal two previously overlooked failure modes caused by length inconsistency in GRPO—entropy collapse (correct long-reasoning patterns are erroneously penalized due to trajectory truncation) and wasted updates / learning tax (shared segments oscillate between positive and negative gradients, squandering computational resources)—harms that go beyond the conventional understanding of “favoring longer/shorter responses.”

  • •

    We propose a new problem perspective and, based on it, establish a sample-construction-based training framework: by proactively constructing equal-length, alignable, and comparable training segments during generation, we replace post-hoc loss corrections on unequal-length responses. Since this framework modifies the inference generation process rather than the loss function, it can be orthogonally combined with algorithm-level improvements such as Dr. GRPO and DAPO.

  • •

    We propose the concrete method EqLen and validate its effectiveness on two architectures, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-Next: it surpasses the strongest baseline by 5.4 percentage points on AIME25 and by 5.8 percentage points on HMMT25, achieves approximately 6×\times generation efficiency improvement (Section 5.2), and reaches 86.4% when combined with DAPO.

2 Related Work

2.1 Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022) has become the standard paradigm for aligning LLMs, with PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) as its canonical implementation. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) replaces the value function with group-relative rewards, substantially reducing training overhead, and has driven breakthrough emergent reasoning capabilities in DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025). However, GRPO’s group-relative comparison mechanism makes it particularly sensitive to trajectory length differences—the core problem addressed in this paper.

2.2 Length Bias in Reinforcement Learning

Length bias has been widely studied in RLHF. Singhal et al. (2023) found that a reward function based solely on length can reproduce most of the downstream improvements of RLHF, revealing the severity of length bias. This problem is especially pronounced in GRPO, where length differences among trajectories within a group directly affect gradient computation.

Algorithm-level corrections. Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025a) identifies two specific sources of bias in GRPO—normalization by sequence length causes long incorrect responses to be insufficiently penalized, and normalization by standard deviation causes questions with extreme reward distributions to be overweighted—and proposes removing both. DAPO (ByteDance Seed, 2025) introduces token-level policy gradient loss and an overlong reward shaping mechanism that penalizes responses exceeding a preset length threshold. GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025a) argues theoretically that applying token-level importance sampling in GRPO is ill-posed because rewards are sequence-level, and therefore lifts clipping, rewards, and optimization entirely to the sequence level. However, LUSPO (Murphy et al., 2026) finds that GSPO further amplifies length bias and corrects this by multiplying each sequence’s loss by its length. P-GSPO (Anonymous, 2025a) introduces a power-law normalization parameter to control how length scales policy updates. DLER (Liu et al., 2025b) revisits simple truncation penalties, finding that accuracy drops stem from insufficient optimization rather than the penalty form itself, and proposes batch-level reward normalization and difficulty-aware truncation. LSPO (Chen et al., 2025) approaches the problem from a data selection perspective, dynamically selecting training data based on average response length. GR3 (Anonymous, 2026) proposes a multiplicative reward scaling paradigm, arguing that additive penalties create compensatory optimization shortcuts.

Reward model-level corrections. Another line of work addresses length bias in the reward model itself. Bu et al. (2025) adaptively adjusts length influence based on query context; FiMi-RM (Anonymous, 2025b) reveals multi-stage nonlinear patterns of bias and fits debiasing models; Kim et al. (2025) uses causal inference for counterfactual data augmentation; Rc-BT (Anonymous, 2025c) decouples semantic preference from length requirements; PAR (Fu et al., 2025) replaces raw rewards with latent preferences. These methods operate solely on the reward model and do not address length bias at the RL optimization level.

Other methods addressing length-related pathologies. Recent work tackles length-related training stability from different mechanistic angles. VESPO (Shen et al., 2026) models the reshaping of sequence-level importance sampling weights as a variational measure-change problem, deriving a closed-form soft suppression kernel ϕ⁡(W)=Wc1⋅ec2​(1−W)\phi(W)=W^{c_{1}}\cdot e^{c_{2}(1-W)} to replace PPO’s hard clipping, avoiding the length bias introduced by 1/T1/T normalization; however, it remains fundamentally a loss-function-level correction—the importance weights of long and short trajectories are inherently coupled with length, and the exponential kernel only smooths the clipping boundary without eliminating the fundamental influence of length on gradient magnitudes. T2T (Lin et al., 2026) proposes capability-aware two-stage length shaping: encouraging longer reasoning to expand the search space when the model answers incorrectly (thickening), and imposing length penalties to encourage conciseness when it answers correctly (thinning); this method’s length regulation depends on the correctness of reward signals and may fail under noisy rewards, and it still builds upon comparisons of unequal-length trajectories. TreeRPO (Yang et al., 2025) achieves PRM-free step-level credit assignment through tree-structured sampling: at each reasoning step, it branches NN candidates to build an NN-ary tree, evaluates leaf nodes, and propagates expected rewards bottom-up; however, its computational cost is O⁡(ND)O(N^{D}) (DD being the tree depth), far exceeding EqLen’s dual-track generation, and it has only been validated on a 1.5B model with unknown scalability. All the above methods alleviate length-related issues from various angles, but none guarantees equal length at the generation mechanism level—this is precisely the unique contribution of EqLen.

Common limitations of existing methods. Table 1 summarizes the comparison across methods. The key observation is that most existing methods perform corrections under the premise of accepting unequal trajectory lengths. This is akin to trying to calibrate a bent ruler—no matter how many correction factors are added, it is never as good as using a straight ruler in the first place. EqLen is that “straight ruler”: it generates equal-length trajectory pairs at the inference framework level, mitigating bias from the generation side.

3 Method

3.1 Preliminaries: GRPO

Given a question qq, the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} independently samples GG trajectories {o1,…,oG}\{o_{1},\ldots,o_{G}\} (e.g., G=16G=16). Each trajectory oio_{i} is scored by a verifiable reward function RR to obtain ri∈{0,1}r_{i}\in\{0,1\}. GRPO computes the advantage via group-level normalization:

A^i=ri−mean​({rj}j=1G)std​({rj}j=1G)\hat{A}_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\text{mean}(\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})}{\text{std}(\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})} (1)

The policy gradient loss of GRPO is:

ℒGRPO=−1G∑i=1G1|oi|∑t=1|oi|[min(ρi,tA^i,clip(ρi,t,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^i)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO}}=-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|o_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_{i}|}\left[\min\left(\rho_{i,t}\hat{A}_{i},\text{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_{i}\right)\right] (2)

where ρi,t=πθ​(oi,t|q,oi,<t)πold​(oi,t|q,oi,<t)\rho_{i,t}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\text{old}}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t})} is the token-level importance ratio and |oi||o_{i}| is the length of trajectory ii.

The source of length bias. The 1|oi|\frac{1}{|o_{i}|} term in Equation 2 is the direct source of length bias. Consider two trajectories oao_{a} (length 50, reward 1) and obo_{b} (length 500, reward 0): the gradient magnitude per token in oao_{a} is 10×\times that of obo_{b}. Even if, as suggested by Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025a), 1|oi|\frac{1}{|o_{i}|} is removed, the sum of gradients across all 500 tokens in the long trajectory obo_{b} still has a far larger absolute value than the sum across 50 tokens in oao_{a}, biasing the optimization toward long trajectories.

This reveals the length bias dilemma: as long as trajectories within a group differ in length, dividing by |oi||o_{i}| biases toward short responses (larger per-token gradients), while not dividing biases toward long responses (larger gradient sums)—the two normalization schemes each have their own bias direction, with no “correct” middle ground.

3.2 Equal-Length Trajectory Generation Framework

Our proposed EqLen generates equal-length trajectory pairs by modifying the inference process itself, eliminating the source of length bias.

3.2.1 Core Mechanism

Parallel dual-track generation. For each question qq, we initialize two trajectories generated in parallel with qq as the shared prefix, decoding synchronously token by token:

at∼πθ(⋅|q,a<t),bt∼πθ(⋅|q,b<t)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|q,a_{<t}),\quad b_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|q,b_{<t}) (3)

The two trajectories are decoded in parallel within the same batch, sharing the KV cache for the question prefix, so the overhead compared to single-trajectory generation is negligible.

Equal-length segment extraction. The two trajectories are generated synchronously. When one trajectory reaches the end-of-sequence token (EOS) first, equal-length segments are extracted from both trajectories up to that point. The trajectory that terminates first is denoted AiA_{i}, and the corresponding equal-length portion from the other trajectory is denoted BiB_{i}. Move the stopped trajectories out of the inference framework, and use the unstopped trajectories as prefixes to launch 2 new continuations. When the next trajectory reaches EOS, equal-length segments Ai+1A_{i+1} and Bi+1B_{i+1} are extracted again, and this cycle repeats until both trajectories have terminated. Using the computational budget for generating two trajectories, we effectively obtain many more trajectory pairs.

Figure 2 provides a concrete example.

3.2.2 Formal Description

The group size is set to GG, and each group is split into subgroups of size 2. Each subgroup’s generation process produces NN equal-length segment pairs {(Ai,Bi)}i=1N\{(A_{i},B_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}. The core invariant is the equal-length constraint:

|Ai|=|Bi|,∀i∈{1,…,N}|A_{i}|=|B_{i}|,\quad\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\} (4)

3.3 Reinforcement Learning with Equal-Length Trajectory Pairs

To avoid notational conflict with the advantage function A^\hat{A}, we henceforth denote each equal-length segment pair (Ai,Bi)(A_{i},B_{i}) as (oi+,oi−)(o_{i}^{+},o_{i}^{-}). Due to the prefix inheritance mechanism, the conditional input for each pair varies with the pair index: the first pair takes the original question qq as input, while the ii-th pair (i≥2i\geq 2) uses xi=q⊕prefixix_{i}=q\oplus\text{prefix}_{i}, where prefixi\text{prefix}_{i} is the inherited prefix sequence. Accordingly, the conditional input for each pair is uniformly denoted as xix_{i} (x1=qx_{1}=q).

Reward computation. For each equal-length segment pair, we use a verifiable reward RR (e.g., answer matching, rubric-based scoring) to evaluate both segments separately. Specifically, oi+o_{i}^{+} is scored directly by RR; the reward for oi−o_{i}^{-} is taken as the maximum reward among all subsequent extension trajectories—if at least one correct trajectory can be generated from oi−o_{i}^{-}, then oi−o_{i}^{-} itself constitutes a valid reasoning path. This design addresses a key deficiency of standard GRPO: in the standard approach, if a trajectory consists of a correct intermediate segment followed by an incorrect continuation, the entire trajectory is judged incorrect, and the correct intermediate segment also receives negative gradients, leading to erroneous updates. Our per-segment evaluation mechanism effectively avoids this issue. We conduct an ablation study comparing the maximum with the mean.

Skip rule. When both segments in a pair receive the same reward, the pair is excluded from gradient updates. This mechanism naturally avoids the entropy collapse and wasted update problems analyzed in Section 4.

Low-cost step-level rewards. Our method effectively splits a single trajectory into multiple segments, each with a distinct reward value, indirectly upgrading outcome-level rewards to step-level rewards.

Given the set of equal-length segment pairs 𝒫={(xi,oi+,oi−)}i=1N\mathcal{P}=\{(x_{i},o_{i}^{+},o_{i}^{-})\}_{i=1}^{N}, each pair constitutes an independent group (group size G′=2G^{\prime}=2), and the advantage is computed separately for each group. Let the rewards be ri+r_{i}^{+} and ri−r_{i}^{-}, and the advantages be A^i+\hat{A}_{i}^{+} and A^i−\hat{A}_{i}^{-}.

The policy gradient loss for each pair simplifies to:

ℒE​q​L​e​n=−12∑s∈{+,−}1|ois|∑t=1|ois|min(ρi,tsA^is,clip(ρi,ts,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^is)\mathcal{L}_{EqLen{}}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s\in\{+,-\}}\frac{1}{|o_{i}^{s}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_{i}^{s}|}\min\left(\rho_{i,t}^{s}\hat{A}_{i}^{s},\text{clip}(\rho_{i,t}^{s},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_{i}^{s}\right) (5)

where ρi,ts=πθ​(oi,ts|xi,oi,<ts)πold​(oi,ts|xi,oi,<ts)\rho_{i,t}^{s}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}^{s}|x_{i},o_{i,<t}^{s})}{\pi_{\text{old}}(o_{i,t}^{s}|x_{i},o_{i,<t}^{s})} is the token-level importance ratio, and the probability for each segment is computed conditioned on its respective input xix_{i}.

For the G/2G/2 subgroups of a given input xx (the original group size GG split into G/2G/2 subgroups of size 2), the kk-th subgroup produces NkN_{k} equal-length segment pairs. The total objective function is:

ℒtotal=1G/2​∑k=1G/21Nk​∑i=1NkℒE​q​L​e​n(k,i)\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\frac{1}{G/2}\sum_{k=1}^{G/2}\frac{1}{N_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{k}}\mathcal{L}_{EqLen{}}^{(k,i)} (6)

where ℒE​q​L​e​n(k,i)\mathcal{L}_{EqLen{}}^{(k,i)} is the loss for the ii-th segment pair in the kk-th subgroup (Equation 5).

The key property of Equation 5: since |oi+|=|oi−||o_{i}^{+}|=|o_{i}^{-}|, the two segments within each pair receive exactly the same scaling regardless of whether the 1|ois|\frac{1}{|o_{i}^{s}|} normalization term is included. This means that length is no longer a variable influencing the relative optimization direction within a group—precisely the goal that Dr. GRPO, GSPO, LUSPO, and other methods attempt but fail to fully achieve.

3.4 Advantages of Prefix Inheritance

Advantages of prefix inheritance. The prefix inheritance mechanism is conceptually consistent with prefix tuning (Li and Liang, 2021), chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022), and prefix-conditioned generation in rejection sampling. Prefix inheritance is equivalent to masking the prefix so that it does not participate in gradient updates, indirectly upgrading outcome-level rewards to step-level rewards.

4 Theoretical Analysis

4.1 Failure Modes from Length Inconsistency

Existing research generally holds that the primary harm of length inconsistency in GRPO is causing model responses to become progressively longer or shorter (length bias), as rigorously proven by Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025a). However, the harms of length inconsistency extend far beyond this. This section proves through constructive counterexamples that GRPO necessarily produces two additional failure modes under certain conditions (complete proofs in Appendix C).

The following analysis is based on the GRPO loss (Equation 2), with G=2G=2, binary rewards r∈{0,1}r\in\{0,1\}, and the PPO clipping term omitted (irrelevant to this paper). The gradient contribution of trajectory ii is gi=−A^i|oi|∑t=1|oi|∇θlogπθ(oi,t|q,oi,<t)g_{i}=-\frac{\hat{A}_{i}}{|o_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_{i}|}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t}).

Proposition 1 (Existence of entropy collapse). There exists a question qq and a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} such that a single GRPO update step strictly decreases the prefix generation probability of a certain correct solution. Intuition: when a short correct trajectory is paired with a long incorrect trajectory (containing a correct prefix), A^2=−1\hat{A}_{2}=-1 causes all tokens of the long trajectory (including the correct prefix) to receive negative gradients. This event has nonzero probability, and its cumulative effect systematically suppresses long-solution patterns.

Proposition 2 (Existence of learning tax). There exists a prefix PP and a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} such that the expected gradient of PP during GRPO training is zero, but the gradient variance is strictly positive. Intuition: when the prefix PP has no predictive power for the final answer (p=0.5p=0.5), the tokens of PP alternately receive positive and negative gradients, yielding 𝔼⁡[gt]=𝟎\mathbb{E}[g_{t}]=\mathbf{0} but Var​(gt)=‖vt‖2/L2>0\text{Var}(g_{t})=\|v_{t}\|^{2}/L^{2}>0, producing O⁡(T)O(\sqrt{T}) parameter drift that constitutes pure noise overhead.

How EqLen avoids these failure modes. EqLen simultaneously eliminates the triggering conditions for both failure modes: (1) inherited prefixes are masked and excluded from gradient computation, so the erroneous penalization in Proposition 1 does not occur; (2) each equal-length segment pair is scored independently, and segments contain no reward-irrelevant shared prefixes, so the gradient oscillation in Proposition 2 does not arise.

5 Experiments

We conduct experiments under a compute-matched setting (equal total GPU hours) on Qwen3-32B (dense) and Qwen3-Next (MoE), evaluating on AIME25, HMMT25, and LiveCodeBench against five baselines: GRPO, Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GSPO, and LUSPO. All experiments use 5 random seeds, reporting means ±\pm 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Full experimental setup details are provided in Appendix A.

5.1 Main Results

Table 2 presents the main experimental results. EqLen achieves the best performance across all benchmarks and model architectures:

Accuracy. On Qwen3-32B, EqLen achieves 84.2% on AIME25 (surpassing the strongest baseline LUSPO by 5.4 percentage points), 64.0% on HMMT25 (+5.8%), and 68.5% on LiveCodeBench (+5.1%). Consistent large improvements are also observed on Qwen3-Next (AIME25: +2.8%, HMMT25: +5.7%, LiveCodeBench: +3.4%), validating the method’s generalization across different model architectures (dense and MoE).

Advantage on long-chain reasoning. EqLen’s advantage is most pronounced on HMMT25, which requires long-chain reasoning (Qwen3-32B: +5.8%, Qwen3-Next: +5.7%). This is because longer reasoning chains exhibit greater trajectory length variation, making length bias more harmful, and EqLen’s equal-length mechanism precisely eliminates this bottleneck.

Training stability. We observe that EqLen’s training curves rise monotonically throughout the training process, without the sharp oscillations commonly seen in standard GRPO and GSPO. This is attributed to the cleaner gradient signals provided by equal-length trajectory pairs, which reduce the gradient noise introduced by length differences.

5.2 Generation Efficiency Analysis

Table 3 shows that EqLen-GRPO achieves approximately 6×\times the sample efficiency of GRPO.

5.3 Ablation Study

Table 4 validates the contribution of each component: (1) Single-pair mode (generation stops when one trajectory terminates without prefix inheritance for continued generation, collecting only one equal-length pair per question) causes a drop on AIME25, as the number of available training pairs is substantially reduced and subsequent steps cannot benefit from contrastive learning; (2) Prefix in gradient (the inherited prefix is not masked and participates in gradient updates) causes a drop, as prefix tokens receive reward signals mismatched with their generation context, introducing noisy gradients that interfere with learned representations; (3) Mean reward (replacing the maximum with the mean over subsequent extension trajectories for the reward of oi−o_{i}^{-}) causes a drop, as the mean is dragged down by incorrect extensions, diluting the positive signal from correct intermediate segments.

5.4 Combination with Existing Methods

EqLen can be orthogonally combined with existing algorithms. On Qwen3-32B (AIME25 Acc avg@32): EqLen-Dr. GRPO reaches 85.1% (+0.9%), and EqLen-DAPO reaches 86.4% (+2.2%), both exceeding EqLen-GRPO’s standalone 84.2%. This demonstrates that equal-length generation mitigates length bias at the generation level, while loss function improvements enhance gradient signal quality—the two are complementary.

6 Discussion and Limitations

Why is equal length so important? The essence of length bias is the coupling between length and reward signals in the loss function. EqLen decouples these two signals by enforcing equal length, so that the model can only obtain optimization reward by improving answer quality.

Limitations and future directions. (1) Our experiments focus on verifiable reward scenarios in mathematical and code reasoning; effectiveness in open-domain generation with reward model-based scoring remains to be validated.

7 Conclusion

This paper proposes EqLen, a method that mitigates length bias in group-relative reinforcement learning at the inference framework level. The core mechanisms—synchronous dual-track generation and prefix inheritance—naturally produce equal-length trajectory pairs, preventing length from interfering with gradient computation. Experiments demonstrate that EqLen outperforms all tested baselines on both Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-Next architectures, and can be orthogonally combined with existing loss function improvements. We believe the paradigm introduced by EqLen also offers insights for addressing other systematic biases in reinforcement learning training, such as difficulty bias and style bias.

Reproducibility Statement

Code will be released via an anonymous repository.

Appendix A Experimental Setup

Overall setting. We compare EqLen against baseline methods under a compute-matched setting (equal total GPU hours). Specifically, using EqLen’s training GPU hours as the reference, each baseline adjusts its number of training steps to consume the same total GPU hours, ensuring a fair comparison. The evaluation metric is Acc avg@32 (average accuracy over 32 independent samples).

Base models. We use Qwen3-32B (dense architecture) and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Thinking (MoE architecture, 3B active parameters), covering both dense and MoE mainstream architectures.

Training data. We use a mixed subset of DeepMath-103K (Zheng et al., 2025b) (decontaminated mathematical reasoning dataset) and OpenCodeReasoning (Dikkala et al., 2025) (decontaminated coding reasoning dataset). The reward function is exact answer matching (r=1r=1 if the final answer is correct, r=0r=0 otherwise), requiring no trained reward model.

Evaluation benchmarks. We cover three types of reasoning tasks: AIME25 (Mathematical Association of America, 2024) (competition mathematics), HMMT25 (Balunović et al., 2025) (long-chain mathematical reasoning), and LiveCodeBench v6 (Jain et al., 2024) (code reasoning).

Baselines. We select 5 representative baselines covering the main technical approaches to length bias mitigation: GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) (standard implementation, G=16G=16), Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025a) (removing length and standard deviation normalization), DAPO (ByteDance Seed, 2025) (token-level loss + overlong reward shaping), GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025a) (sequence-level optimization), and LUSPO (Murphy et al., 2026) (length-scaled GSPO correction).

Implementation details. All methods use the same training and inference hyperparameters. All experiments are run with 5 random seeds, reporting means ±\pm 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

Appendix B Hyperparameter Configuration

Training hyperparameters. All methods use the same configuration: AdamW optimizer (20-step warmup), learning rate 1×10−61\times 10^{-6} (Qwen3-32B) / 5×10−75\times 10^{-7} (Qwen3-Next), KL penalty βkl=0.002\beta_{\text{kl}}=0.002, maximum sequence length 32768, prompt batch size 64. Qwen3-32B is trained on 8×\timesA100 80GB, and Qwen3-Next on 16×\timesA100 80GB.

Inference settings. Temperature = 0.6, TopP = 0.95, TopK = 20, MinP = 0. All methods are compared under the same decoding settings, ensuring that differences stem solely from the training method. All evaluations use 32 independent samples to compute avg@32.

Seeds and statistics. All experiments are run with 5 random seeds, reporting means ±\pm 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

EqLen-specific configuration. Sampling group size G=16G=16 (split into 8 subgroups of size 2); each question generates one dual-track stream, with each subgroup producing approximately 6 equal-length pairs on average.

Appendix C Complete Proofs of Propositions 1 and 2

C.1 Proof of Proposition 1 (Existence of Entropy Collapse)

Proposition 1. There exists a question qq and a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} such that a single GRPO (G=2G=2) update step strictly decreases the prefix generation probability of a certain correct solution.

Proof. We adopt the equal-length segment notation from EqLen. Let two trajectories be generated in parallel, producing equal-length segment pairs (Ai,Bi)(A_{i},B_{i}) where |Ai|=|Bi||A_{i}|=|B_{i}| (AiA_{i} denotes the segment that first reaches EOS, BiB_{i} denotes the corresponding equal-length counterpart). Let question qq admit three possible responses:

  • •

    A1A_{1}: the first segment directly yields the correct answer (first to reach EOS), r=1r=1, length |A1||A_{1}|

  • •

    B1+A2B_{1}+A_{2}: B1B_{1} is equal-length to A1A_{1} (|B1|=|A1||B_{1}|=|A_{1}|) and serves as a valid reasoning prefix; A2A_{2} is the subsequent segment but ultimately gives an incorrect answer, r=0r=0, total length |B1|+|A2||B_{1}|+|A_{2}|

  • •

    B1+B2+A3B_{1}+B_{2}+A_{3}: shares the same prefix B1B_{1} (|B1|=|A1||B_{1}|=|A_{1}|), B2B_{2} is equal-length to A2A_{2} (|B2|=|A2||B_{2}|=|A_{2}|), A3A_{3} is the third segment that gives the correct answer, r=1r=1, total length |B1|+|B2|+|A3||B_{1}|+|B_{2}|+|A_{3}|

Here B1B_{1} is a valid reasoning prefix (e.g., a problem modeling step such as “let xx be…”), shared by both the correct response B1+B2+A3B_{1}+B_{2}+A_{3} and the incorrect response B1+A2B_{1}+A_{2}.

How GRPO handles this. Standard GRPO treats entire trajectories as units, sampling G=2G=2 trajectories and computing advantages from sequence-level rewards. Consider the following sampling outcome (this event has nonzero probability under πθ\pi_{\theta}): o1=A1o_{1}=A_{1} (correct, r1=1r_{1}=1) and o2=B1+A2o_{2}=B_{1}+A_{2} (incorrect, r2=0r_{2}=0). The two trajectories have unequal lengths: |o1|=|A1||o_{1}|=|A_{1}|, |o2|=|B1|+|A2|=|A1|+|A2||o_{2}|=|B_{1}|+|A_{2}|=|A_{1}|+|A_{2}|.

From r1=1,r2=0r_{1}=1,r_{2}=0, Equation 1 yields A^2=−1\hat{A}_{2}=-1. GRPO uniformly broadcasts this advantage to every token of o2o_{2}. The gradient contribution from o2o_{2} is:

g2=1|o2|​∑t=1|o2|∇θ​log​πθ​(o2,t|q,o2,<t)g_{2}=\frac{1}{|o_{2}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_{2}|}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(o_{2,t}|q,o_{2,<t}) (7)

The critical issue: within o2=B1+A2o_{2}=B_{1}+A_{2}, the first |B1|=|A1||B_{1}|=|A_{1}| tokens of prefix B1B_{1} are entirely correct reasoning steps, yet because A^2=−1\hat{A}_{2}=-1 is broadcast to the entire trajectory, every token in B1B_{1} receives negative gradients.

The parameter update is θ′=θ−η​g2\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\eta g_{2} (η>0\eta>0). For any token btb_{t} in B1B_{1} (t≤|B1|t\leq|B_{1}|), by the positive-definiteness of the Fisher information matrix:

∇θlogπθ(bt|⋅)⊤g2≥1|o2|∥∇θlogπθ(bt|⋅)∥2>0\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(b_{t}|\cdot)^{\top}g_{2}\geq\frac{1}{|o_{2}|}\|\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(b_{t}|\cdot)\|^{2}>0 (8)

Therefore πθ′​(bt|q,b<t)<πθ​(bt|q,b<t)\pi_{\theta^{\prime}}(b_{t}|q,b_{<t})<\pi_{\theta}(b_{t}|q,b_{<t}): the generation probability of prefix B1B_{1} is strictly decreased. When the pairing (A1,B1+A2)(A_{1},\;B_{1}+A_{2}) is repeatedly encountered during training, B1B_{1} is penalized again and again, causing all solutions starting with B1B_{1}—including the correct solution B1+B2+A3B_{1}+B_{2}+A_{3}—to be systematically suppressed. The model gradually loses the ability to reach correct answers through long reasoning chains, and policy diversity declines—i.e., entropy collapse.

How EqLen avoids this. EqLen does not operate on entire trajectories but instead independently evaluates each equal-length segment pair (Ai,Bi)(A_{i},B_{i}). In the above construction, EqLen evaluates (A1,B1)(A_{1},B_{1}) as the first pair and (A2,B2)(A_{2},B_{2}) as the second pair separately. For the first pair, A1A_{1} is correct, and B1B_{1}’s reward is taken as the maximum reward among all its subsequent extended trajectories, so B1B_{1} is not erroneously penalized and receives the correct reward. When B1B_{1} serves as an inherited prefix, it is masked and excluded from gradient computation. Therefore B1B_{1} is never penalized due to A2A_{2}’s error, and the failure mode of Proposition 1 does not occur. □\square

C.2 Proof of Proposition 2 (Existence of Learning Tax)

Proposition 2. There exists a shared prefix B1B_{1} and a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} such that the expected gradient of B1B_{1} during GRPO training is zero, but the gradient variance is strictly positive—i.e., B1B_{1} receives no effective learning signal yet continuously consumes optimizer resources.

Proof. We continue with the construction and equal-length segment notation from Proposition 1. Question qq has three responses: A1A_{1} (correct), B1+A2B_{1}+A_{2} (incorrect), B1+B2+A3B_{1}+B_{2}+A_{3} (correct), where |Ai|=|Bi||A_{i}|=|B_{i}|. Let the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} intermittently sample trajectories containing prefix B1B_{1}.

In GRPO with G=2G=2, B1B_{1} alternately receives opposing gradient signals under different pairings (when r=r′r=r^{\prime}, A^=0\hat{A}=0 and no update occurs; we ignore this case):

  1. 1.

    B1B_{1} is penalized: the pair (A1,B1+A2)(A_{1},\;B_{1}+A_{2}) is sampled. The entire B1+A2B_{1}+A_{2} is incorrect (r=0r=0), A1A_{1} is correct (r′=1r^{\prime}=1), so A^=−1\hat{A}=-1 is broadcast to every token of B1+A2B_{1}+A_{2}. The gradient contribution of each token btb_{t} in B1B_{1} is gt(−)=+1|B1|+|A2|∇θlogπθ(bt|⋅)g_{t}^{(-)}=+\frac{1}{|B_{1}|+|A_{2}|}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(b_{t}|\cdot) (decreasing B1B_{1}’s probability).

  2. 2.

    B1B_{1} is rewarded: the pair (B1+A2,B1+B2+A3)(B_{1}+A_{2},\;B_{1}+B_{2}+A_{3}) is sampled. B1+B2+A3B_{1}+B_{2}+A_{3} is correct (r=1r=1), B1+A2B_{1}+A_{2} is incorrect (r′=0r^{\prime}=0), so A^=+1\hat{A}=+1 is broadcast to every token of B1+B2+A3B_{1}+B_{2}+A_{3}. The gradient contribution of each token btb_{t} in B1B_{1} is gt(+)=−1|B1|+|B2|+|A3|∇θlogπθ(bt|⋅)g_{t}^{(+)}=-\frac{1}{|B_{1}|+|B_{2}|+|A_{3}|}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(b_{t}|\cdot) (increasing B1B_{1}’s probability).

Let L(−)=|B1|+|A2|L^{(-)}=|B_{1}|+|A_{2}|, L(+)=|B1|+|B2|+|A3|L^{(+)}=|B_{1}|+|B_{2}|+|A_{3}|, and vt=∇θlogπθ(bt|⋅)v_{t}=\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(b_{t}|\cdot). Let the two cases occur with probabilities pp and 1−p1-p respectively. When pL(−)=1−pL(+)\frac{p}{L^{(-)}}=\frac{1-p}{L^{(+)}} (i.e., p=L(−)L(−)+L(+)p=\frac{L^{(-)}}{L^{(-)}+L^{(+)}}):

𝔼⁡[gt]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[g_{t}] =p⋅vtL(−)+(1−p)⋅(−vtL(+))=𝟎\displaystyle=p\cdot\frac{v_{t}}{L^{(-)}}+(1-p)\cdot\left(-\frac{v_{t}}{L^{(+)}}\right)=\mathbf{0} (9)

Yet the gradient variance is strictly positive:

Var​(gt)\displaystyle\text{Var}(g_{t}) =𝔼⁡[‖gt‖2]=p⋅‖vt‖2(L(−))2+(1−p)⋅‖vt‖2(L(+))2>0\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\|g_{t}\|^{2}]=p\cdot\frac{\|v_{t}\|^{2}}{(L^{(-)})^{2}}+(1-p)\cdot\frac{\|v_{t}\|^{2}}{(L^{(+)})^{2}}>0 (10)

Prefix B1B_{1} is repeatedly penalized and rewarded during training: penalized when the pair (A1,B1+A2)(A_{1},\;B_{1}+A_{2}) is encountered, rewarded when the pair (B1+A2,B1+B2+A3)(B_{1}+A_{2},\;B_{1}+B_{2}+A_{3}) is encountered, yet the expected gradient is zero—B1B_{1} learns no effective signal. However, the per-step gradient variance is strictly positive, causing parameters to oscillate between positive and negative directions. Over TT training steps, the standard deviation of cumulative parameter drift is O⁡(T)O(\sqrt{T}) (random walk), producing ineffective parameter drift that consumes optimizer momentum and learning budget, constituting a learning tax.

How EqLen avoids this. In EqLen, each equal-length segment pair (Ai,Bi)(A_{i},B_{i}) is independently evaluated, and the inherited prefix B1B_{1} is masked and excluded from gradient computation. In the second pair (A2,B2)(A_{2},B_{2}), A2A_{2} and B2B_{2} are equal-length and independently scored, so sequence-level rewards are not back-propagated to irrelevant prefixes. Therefore B1B_{1} never receives contradictory gradients, and the learning tax of Proposition 2 does not occur. □\square

Appendix D Derivation of EqLen Integrated into RLOO

This section derives the complete loss function when EqLen’s equal-length generation mechanism is integrated into the RLOO (Kool et al., 2019) framework.

D.1 Standard RLOO

RLOO (Kool et al., 2019) samples GG independent trajectories {o1,…,oG}\{o_{1},\ldots,o_{G}\} for each question xx and computes the advantage using a leave-one-out mean as the baseline:

A^iRLOO=ri−1G−1​∑j≠irj\hat{A}_{i}^{\text{RLOO}}=r_{i}-\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j\neq i}r_{j} (11)

The corresponding token-level policy gradient loss is:

ℒRLOO=−1G∑i=1G1|oi|∑t=1|oi|A^iRLOOlogπθ(oi,t|x,oi,<t)\mathcal{L}_{\text{RLOO}}=-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|o_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_{i}|}\hat{A}_{i}^{\text{RLOO}}\log\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}|x,o_{i,<t}) (12)

The advantage of RLOO is that it does not require standard deviation normalization (cf. GRPO’s Equation 1), but the 1|oi|\frac{1}{|o_{i}|} term in Equation 12 still applies different scaling to trajectories of different lengths, so length bias persists.

D.2 Integrating Equal-Length Generation

The GG trajectories are split into G/2G/2 subgroups of size 2. Each subgroup produces NkN_{k} equal-length segment pairs {(ok,i+,ok,i−)}i=1Nk\{(o_{k,i}^{+},o_{k,i}^{-})\}_{i=1}^{N_{k}} through EqLen’s synchronous dual-track generation and prefix inheritance mechanism, satisfying |ok,i+|=|ok,i−|=Lk,i|o_{k,i}^{+}|=|o_{k,i}^{-}|=L_{k,i}.

Applying RLOO with G′=2G^{\prime}=2 independently to each equal-length segment pair (Equation 11), the advantage simplifies to:

A^k,i+=rk,i+−rk,i−,A^k,i−=rk,i−−rk,i+\hat{A}_{k,i}^{+}=r_{k,i}^{+}-r_{k,i}^{-},\qquad\hat{A}_{k,i}^{-}=r_{k,i}^{-}-r_{k,i}^{+} (13)

When rk,i+=rk,i−r_{k,i}^{+}=r_{k,i}^{-}, A^k,i±=0\hat{A}_{k,i}^{\pm}=0 and the gradient is naturally zero, which is consistent with EqLen’s skip rule—no additional mechanism is needed.

D.3 EqLen-RLOO Loss Function

Substituting Equation 13 into the RLOO loss (Equation 12) and expanding for each equal-length segment pair:

ℒEqLen-RLOO(k,i)=−12∑s∈{+,−}1Lk,i∑t=1Lk,iA^k,islogπθ(ok,i,ts|xk,i,ok,i,<ts)\mathcal{L}_{\text{EqLen-RLOO}}^{(k,i)}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s\in\{+,-\}}\frac{1}{L_{k,i}}\sum_{t=1}^{L_{k,i}}\hat{A}_{k,i}^{s}\log\pi_{\theta}(o_{k,i,t}^{s}|x_{k,i},o_{k,i,<t}^{s}) (14)

where xk,ix_{k,i} is the conditional input for the ii-th pair in the kk-th subgroup (including the inherited prefix). Since |ok,i+|=|ok,i−|=Lk,i|o_{k,i}^{+}|=|o_{k,i}^{-}|=L_{k,i}, 1Lk,i\frac{1}{L_{k,i}} applies exactly the same scaling to o+o^{+} and o−o^{-}—length bias is eliminated.

Aggregating across all subgroups and segment pairs, the total loss is:

ℒEqLen-RLOO=1G/2​∑k=1G/21Nk​∑i=1NkℒEqLen-RLOO(k,i)\mathcal{L}_{\text{EqLen-RLOO}}=\frac{1}{G/2}\sum_{k=1}^{G/2}\frac{1}{N_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{k}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{EqLen-RLOO}}^{(k,i)} (15)

D.4 Relationship to EqLen-GRPO

Comparing Equation 14 with the EqLen-GRPO loss (Equation 5), the differences are limited to:

  1. 1.

    Advantage function: RLOO uses A^s=rs−rs¯\hat{A}^{s}=r^{s}-r^{\bar{s}} (no standard deviation normalization), while GRPO uses A^s=(rs−r¯)/σr\hat{A}^{s}=(r^{s}-\bar{r})/\sigma_{r}. Under binary rewards r∈{0,1}r\in\{0,1\} with r+≠r−r^{+}\neq r^{-}, both reduce to ±1\pm 1, making them exactly equivalent.

  2. 2.

    PPO clipping: EqLen-GRPO includes the clipping mechanism min⁡(ρt​A^,clip​(ρt,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​A^)\min(\rho_{t}\hat{A},\text{clip}(\rho_{t},1{-}\epsilon,1{+}\epsilon)\hat{A}), while pure RLOO does not. In practice, clipping can be freely added for enhanced stability.

Therefore, under binary rewards, EqLen-RLOO and EqLen-GRPO are identical in their advantage signals, with PPO clipping as an optional stability enhancement. The structure of the total loss (Equations 15 and 6) is also identical, demonstrating that EqLen’s equal-length generation mechanism can serve as a plug-and-play module that seamlessly integrates into different policy optimization frameworks such as RLOO and GRPO.
